rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Kingdom Monera comprises prokaryotic organisms: bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma, and archaebacteria. Bacteria show diverse shapes, nutrition, and reproduction (binary fission + genetic exchange). The growth curve (lag, log, stationary, death) and Gram staining are fundamental microbiology tools. Cyanobacteria fix nitrogen and photosynthesise.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Binary fission: 1 cell → 2 identical daughter cells (asexual)
Growth curve: N(t) = N₀ × 2ⁿ (n = number of generations in log phase)
Lag → Log → Stationary → Death

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Bacteria are prokaryotic: they have no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.  ·  Cyanobacteria are bacteria (prokaryotes), NOT algae; they fix nitrogen but are not "true" algae.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB expects a labelled bacterium diagram plus the growth curve.  ·  Gram-staining differentiation (+ve vs -ve) is a very common short-answer.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Escherichia coli — rod-shaped, Gram-negative, model organism for genetics.  ·  Lactobacillus — rod, used in curd/cheese making (lactic acid fermentation).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall; it is the smallest known living cell.  ·  Archaea differ from Bacteria in cell wall (no peptidoglycan) and membrane lipids; they live in extreme environments.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Label a bacterium  ·  Draw the growth curve

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Monera = M-O-N (Micro, Osmotic, No nucleus).  ·  Shapes: Cocci = round; Bacilli = rod; Spirilla = spiral.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Why are bacteria called "prokaryotes"?  ·  Differentiate the four phases of the bacterial growth curve.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Draw and label a typical bacterium — very common.  ·  Describe the bacterial growth curve (4 phases).

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Prokaryotic cell structure  ·  Bacterial shapes  ·  Nutrition modes  ·  Growth curve

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Monera = prokaryotic: no true nucleus, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA.  ·  Shapes: cocci, bacilli, spirilla; arrangements: diplo-, strepto-, staphylo-.  ·  Nutrition: autotrophic (photo/chemo) + heterotrophic (saprophytes, parasites).  ·  Growth curve: lag, log, stationary, death.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Bacteria are the oldest life form on Earth (~3.5 billion years).  ·  A single bacterial cell can divide in ~20 minutes under optimal conditions (E. coli).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Explain the Gram-staining test and its significance.  ·  What are the different shapes of bacteria with one example each?  ·  State the ecological importance of bacteria (decomposition, nitrogen cycle, symbiosis).

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Explain Gram-staining and differentiate +ve and -ve.  ·  Tabulate bacterial shapes and arrangements.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Nostoc / Anabaena — cyanobacteria, filamentous, nitrogen-fixing in rice fields.  ·  Mycoplasma pneumoniae — smallest living cell (no cell wall), causes atypical pneumonia.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The smallest known living cell is: → B  ·  The cell wall of most bacteria is made of: → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Kingdom Monera: prokaryotic organisms (no membrane-bound nucleus); includes bacteria, cyanobacteria (blue-green algae), mycoplasma, and archaebacteria.  ·  Bacterial cell: capsule (slime layer) → cell wall (peptidoglycan) → plasma membrane → cytoplasm; 70S ribosomes; naked circular DNA (nucleoid); may have pili, fimbriae, flagella, mesosomes.  ·  Shapes: cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod), spirilla/spirochaetes (spiral). Arrangements: diplococci, streptococci, staphylococci.

rows.text: Binary fission  ·  Genetic exchange  ·  Cyanobacteria

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Gram staining  ·  Gram +ve: thick peptidoglycan → retains crystal violet (purple); Gram -ve: thin + LPS → pink (safranin)  ·  Binary fission = asexual reproduction; conjugation/transformation/transduction = genetic exchange.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Cyanobacteria: photosynthetic + nitrogen-fixing (Nostoc, Anabaena).  ·  Gram stain: +ve (purple, thick wall) vs -ve (pink, thin wall + LPS).  ·  Binary fission produces two genetically identical daughter cells; conjugation transfers DNA but does not increase cell number.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Gram-positive bacteria have a THICK peptidoglycan layer; Gram-negative have a THIN layer plus an outer LPS membrane (more resistant to many antibiotics).  ·  Cyanobacteria (Nostoc, Anabaena) and their nitrogen-fixing role are frequently asked.  ·  Mention Mycoplasma as the smallest living cell and its lack of a cell wall.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Memorise bacterial shapes and arrangements with examples.  ·  Learn the 4 phases of the bacterial growth curve.  ·  Draw and label a bacterium from memory.
